newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan city returns to normal after Taleban rout.
newsitem.headline: Afghan city returns to normal after Taleban rout.

text.p: Life was returning to normal in the war-ravaged northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Thursday, a day after the rout of its Taleban Islamic militia captors by local Afghan forces.
Shops reopened and people returned to the streets apparently happy by the retreat of the Taleban fighters only after 72 hours in the city.
Witnesses said bodies of Taleban fighters and burned-out trucks and other vehicles lay in the streets of Mazar-i-Sharif, now firmly in control of ethnic Uzbek troops of General Abdul Malik.
Malik turned on the militia on Tuesday, only eight days after striking an alliance with them amid a mutiny he staged against opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who later fled to Turkey.
There were a few charred buildings and shops but there were more people on the streets than there had been before Mazar-i-Sharif fell to Malik's troops on Saturday.
"Shops are reopening, people are relaxed and happy that the Taleban are out of the town," a resident said.
In the Shi'ite Moslem district of Saidabad the bodies of eight Taleban fighters lay piled on the ground awaiting collection by a vehicle from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
"This is what happens to every foreigner who comes to the north," Ahmed Ali, a resident of Saidabad, said.
Outside the foreign ministry there were the remnants of a truck whose cargo of ammunition had exploded during the battle.

"The Pakistanis were very happy when their ambassador came to Mazar, it was a celebration for Pakistan, now they are crying because of what happened to the Taleban," another resident, Amir Shah, said.
"All the people in the town were fighting the Taleban," he added.
Residents were visibly delighted to see the back of the Taleban, who only arrived on Sunday but wasted little time in trying to impose their strict version of Islam on the city.
Swarming through Mazar-i-Sharif in white-flagged vehicles, they broadcast orders that men should grow beards, women should stay at home and girls should stop going to school.
Another resident, Muhammad Zuhair, accused the militia of being supported by Pakistan and the United States.
"Our message to the United States, the Pakistanis and the Arabs is that don't interfere in Afghan affairs, let us make our own choice about our own government," Zuhair said.
Pakistan has openly backed the radical militia and was the first of three countries to accord formal diplomatic recognition to the Taleban government after the capture of Mazar-i-Sharif.
The defeated Taleban left the city towards the southeast on Wednesday heading towards the town of Pul-i-Khumri in Baghlan province and were chased by Malik's tanks and military vehicles.
It was not known what happened afterwards.

Pul-i-Khumri, lying on the main highway from the capital Kabul to north Afghanistan via the strategic Salang Pass, was captured by the Taleban on Wednesday from forces of Syed Jafar Naderi, allied to the Dostum-led opposition alliance.
The United Nations was on Thursday planning to evacuate about 70 foreigners, including journalists and aid workers, by road through the Uzbek border town of Termez.
